plot_extraction.response_text:
On Christmas Eve in Chicago, a starving, destitute twenty-four-year-old estranged from his family concludes that he has failed at every pursuit and contemplates suicide. Driven by hunger, he decides to become a thief. After instinctively returning a dropped package to a young woman, he slips into a wealthy home during a party and steals jewelry from an upstairs bedroom.

While searching the room, he discovers the silver cup he used as a child and realizes he has unknowingly entered his own family’s new home. His mother finds him, recognizes him immediately, and embraces him despite his ashamed confession that he came to rob the house. She insists he cannot steal what is already his and persuades his stern father to accept him back. After speaking privately with his son, the father agrees that he may stay.

His mother feeds him, comforts him, and refuses to demand an account of his years of wandering and failure. She tells him that love requires neither pardon nor explanation. Resting beside the fire in familiar surroundings, he feels safe for the first time in years and begins to believe that his ruined life may yet be redeemed.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story uses a late nineteenth-century realist style softened by sentiment, melodrama, and moral romance. Its opening is concrete and urban: precise Chicago street names, Christmas traffic, slush, cold, hunger, saloons, free lunches, pawning, and casual employment establish a recognizable social world. Against this documentary surface, the narrative develops into a providential homecoming tale. The plot moves from destitution and contemplated suicide, through attempted theft and sudden recognition, to food, familial reconciliation, and spiritual hope. Coincidence is therefore not concealed but embraced as the mechanism of emotional and moral resolution.

The narration is third-person and largely centered on William’s consciousness. It begins with an external view of “two very shabby looking young men,” then moves into sustained free indirect discourse and authorial reflection. William’s memories, self-accusations, bodily sensations, and sardonic thoughts frequently merge with the narrator’s voice. At intervals, the narrator broadens his case into general claims about human experience, as in the reflections on hunger, failure, introspection, crime, love, and forgiveness. This produces an omniscient, morally interpretive voice rather than a neutral or strictly psychological one. The narrator is sympathetic to the protagonist but does not idealize him: William is presented as intelligent, cultivated, self-dramatizing, weak-willed, and genuinely culpable, while also being shaped by poverty and emotional exhaustion.

The prose alternates between expansive introspection and rapid dramatic action. Descriptive and reflective passages often use long, cumulative sentences with parallel clauses and repeated syntactic patterns. Lists are especially prominent: vehicles in the street, vanished pleasures, failed occupations, birthday foods, former ambitions, and the “flimsy sophistries” of Bohemian life accumulate to convey both social abundance and personal waste. These long movements are punctuated by short emphatic statements such as “A man’s got to eat,” “Tonight was his birthday, too,” and “His was a very common one.” Such compression gives key judgments an aphoristic force. Exclamations, rhetorical questions, sentence fragments, and direct addresses intensify the emotional climaxes.

The diction combines elevated literary language with colloquial American speech. The narrator uses abstract and figurative terms such as “introspection,” “ineffaceable failures,” “unyielding conviction,” and “mental distortion,” while the opening dialogue includes period slang and contractions: “hock,” “bone him,” “no show,” “folks,” “ain’t,” and “loaf around.” This contrast helps distinguish William’s immediate social degradation from the refinement of his education and inner life. His own speech shifts accordingly. With his companion he is dry, evasive, and ironic; with his mother he becomes formal, broken, and confessional. The dialogue is often emotionally explicit, particularly in the family scenes, and characters state their motives and feelings more openly than would be usual in restrained modern realism.

Figurative language is abundant and frequently organized around cold, darkness, exhaustion, and enclosure. Failure closes around William “like the walls” of a torture chamber; despair becomes a “Pale Spectre,” night, granite, and sealed coral cells; stale memories resemble trapped cigarette smoke, flat champagne, and an overused song. By contrast, home and maternal love are expressed through warmth, fragrance, fire, food, touch, and shelter. The movement from the wet street to the illuminated house, then to dinner and the fireside chair, gives the story a strong symbolic architecture: physical passage inward corresponds to emotional restoration. Hunger is both literal and moral, while eating becomes evidence that William has re-entered human fellowship.

The story also relies on recurring objects as emotional triggers. The lost package tests William’s capacity for theft; the silver childhood mug produces recognition; the old chair reconnects the ruined adult with the hopeful child he once was. These objects compress backstory into moments of dramatic revelation. The childhood mug is especially effective because it turns the intended burglary into an unconscious return home before William knows where he is. His instinctive removal of his hat while entering as a burglar performs a similar function: inherited manners and identity survive beneath his attempted criminal role.

Irony shapes both characterization and plot. William treats his own ruin as one more aesthetic or intellectual experiment, imagining labels such as “the failure as a journalist” and “the failure as a thief.” His allusions to the “Dance of Death” and “Childe Roland” reveal education, theatricality, and habitual self-observation even at the brink of disaster. The central situational irony is that he tries to steal property that is legally and emotionally “his own.” The mother’s answer—“How could you rob your own house?”—redefines the apparent crime as a distorted attempt to reclaim belonging. This irony is ultimately benevolent rather than punitive.

Characterization is built through contrast. William’s elegant sensibility conflicts with his shabby appearance and degraded circumstances. His mother is rendered in idealized, almost monumental terms: beautiful, intuitive, physically strong, and capable of unconditional love. The father is restrained, proud, and emotionally inarticulate, but not cruel; his terse admission that he “failed” with his son parallels William’s own obsession with failure and permits reconciliation without a prolonged confrontation. The mother mediates between them and serves as the story’s emotional and ethical center. Her language elevates love above judgment, pardon, and even explanation.

The setting is strongly seasonal and symbolic. Christmas Eve supplies crowded streets, conspicuous wealth, childhood memories, bells, family reunion, and an implied pattern of rebirth. William’s birthday falling on Christmas Eve reinforces the motif of a second birth. The prosperous house amid urban misery sharpens the social contrast, but the story does not develop into a systemic critique of class. William briefly feels a starving man’s hatred of wealth, yet the resolution restores him to his affluent family rather than questioning the social order. Poverty is treated with vivid sympathy, but the final solution is personal, familial, and providential.

The emotional register rises steadily from bleak irony to overt pathos. Repetitions such as “hard, hard,” “loves, and loves and loves,” and the mother’s repeated use of “my boy” and “my son” are designed for direct emotional impact. Physical gestures—embracing, struggling, bowing the head, kneeling, clasping hands, kissing—carry much of the climax. The sentiment is earnest and unguarded, though it is moderated by William’s grim humor and shame. His wit prevents the earlier despair from becoming wholly lachrymose; once his mother recognizes him, however, the story willingly enters melodrama.

The ending expands from domestic reconciliation into religious-philosophical speculation. Chimes, sleep, dawn, the Author, the Potter, and “Things of Clay” frame human weakness within a possible divine design. The conclusion does not assert a rigid doctrine so much as voice a weary hope that evil and failure may be temporary distortions rather than final truths. This gives the story a characteristic arc from social realism through sentimental recognition to metaphysical consolation.

Mechanically, the text reflects older usage and transmission conventions. It favors “O” rather than “Oh,” sometimes omits punctuation that contemporary prose would supply, and uses period-specific vocabulary and racial terminology in dialogue. Paragraphs are often substantial during introspection but shorten sharply at dramatic moments. Overall, the style is urban-realist in detail, romantic in symbolism, melodramatic in construction, psychologically sympathetic in viewpoint, and explicitly redemptive in its moral vision.

generation.response_text:
At the corner of Clark and Randolph Streets, where the cable-cars clanged and shivered through ridges of blackened snow, two very shabby-looking young men stood beneath the awning of a closed cigar shop and watched Chicago prepare for Christmas.

The city was in no mood to notice them. Carriages rolled northward toward warm houses; express wagons jolted among omnibuses; sleigh-bells sounded fitfully where the slush permitted runners to scrape the buried pavement. Women with bright cheeks and burdened arms hurried under umbrellas, guarding parcels of toys, cakes, ribbons, books, slippers, smoking-jackets, dolls, and the innumerable small absurdities by which affection seeks to prove itself at the end of the year. Every saloon door breathed light, tobacco smoke, wet wool, and roast meat into the storm.

“Got anything left to hock?” asked the shorter of the two men.

“Nothing portable,” replied William Arden. “My education is extensive, but the brokers refuse to advance on it.”

His companion laughed without mirth. “You might bone Harrison for a five.”

“Harrison has been boned to the marrow.”

“What about the newspaper fellows?”

“They cherish me as a memory.”

“Then there ain’t no show?”

“There is always Lake Michigan.”

The shorter man glanced at him, uncertain whether the answer were a joke. William’s jokes had lately acquired an unpleasant edge. They were like thin ice over deep water: a man smiled at the glitter and hesitated to put his foot upon it.

“Well,” the other said, thrusting his hands deeper into his pockets, “I’m going down to Billy Ryan’s. They put out a free lunch at six. Maybe I can stand off the bartender.”

“You owe him money.”

“That’s why I know him. Coming?”

William shook his head.

“You’d better. A man’s got to eat.”

“Yes,” said William, “that is one of Nature’s coarser arguments.”

The young man moved away, was swallowed by the crowd, reappeared beneath a lamp, and disappeared again. William remained under the awning.

He was twenty-four years old that day.

The circumstance possessed no great importance, except that birthdays, like milestones and gravestones, persuade a man to measure the road behind him. At twenty-four Alexander had conquered something considerable; Byron had made Europe discuss his wickedness; Keats had nearly completed his brief bargain with immortality. William Arden had conquered a second-hand overcoat, inspired several creditors to profanity, and written a comic paragraph about a Polish alderman which had been cut to three lines and printed without his initials.

He had not eaten since the previous morning.

Hunger, when it is mentioned at a comfortable table, appears a simple appetite, almost a humorous inconvenience. Men who have never lacked food talk of fasting as if the stomach were a peevish child to be disciplined. But hunger prolonged becomes first a pain, then a fever, then a cold intelligence which occupies the whole body and turns every faculty toward itself. It lodges behind the eyes; it trembles in the fingers; it scents bread through brick walls; it makes the universe revolve about a plate.

William had passed beyond the lively period of hunger. He was weak, chilled, and curiously detached. The steaming windows of restaurants no longer tortured him with distinct visions. Beef, oysters, coffee, buckwheat cakes, turkey, mince-pie—all the vanished splendors of nourishment had blended into one golden unreality, as the pleasures of childhood blend into a summer afternoon which perhaps never existed.

He walked north on Clark Street because standing still required more resolution than walking.

The snow had turned to rain, and the rain, meeting the filth of traffic, became an adhesive gray substance which splashed his trousers and entered through a separation in his right shoe. His collar was clean only in intention; his gloves had no fellowship with one another; his overcoat, once black, had faded to the greenish hue of old bronze. Yet he carried himself erect. There are men whose poverty cries aloud from every seam, and others whose ruin wears the air of an eccentric costume. William belonged to the latter sort. His face was thin and cultivated; his mouth sensitive, sardonic, and weak; his eyes dark with intelligence, sleeplessness, and the habit of examining his own emotions while suffering them.

He had failed at everything.

The thought did not come newly. It had been with him for months, following him from lodging-house to lodging-house, waiting beside him in newspaper offices, sitting opposite him in cheap restaurants when he could still afford them. But on this night it closed around him with the completeness of four granite walls.

He had failed at college, not through stupidity, but through a brilliant incapacity for submission. He had failed in his father’s office, because figures bored him and punctuality seemed a conspiracy against the imagination. He had failed as an actor, though for six intoxicating weeks he had carried a spear and one sentence through Iowa. He had failed as a poet, a lecturer, a clerk, a canvasser for an encyclopedia, a teacher of elocution, a political reporter, and secretary to a gentleman who sold patent furnaces and later removed to Canada without taking his liabilities. He had loved two women: one wisely declined to ruin herself; the other accepted a jeweler’s proposal while William was composing a letter explaining why marriage was a bourgeois institution. He had borrowed, promised, postponed, deceived, repented, and borrowed again.

His was a very common tragedy.

Because his tastes were refined, he had mistaken them for character. Because he understood noble actions, he had assumed himself capable of performing them. He could analyze courage in five pages, discuss duty until midnight, and quote the martyrs over beer; but when morning demanded that he rise, endure dullness, keep faith, and do one small honest thing repeatedly, his soul protested against the vulgarity of the arrangement.

At first he had called his wanderings experience. Then he called them Bohemianism. After that he called them bad luck. Tonight he called them by their name.

Failure.

The word walked beside him.

He turned eastward. From a church near Dearborn Street came the practice of Christmas music, uncertain at first, then gathering into a grave sweetness above the traffic. The sound brought him, with cruel simplicity, a room he had not seen for five years: holly over a mantel, wax candles upon a tree, his mother’s hands moving among packages, his father pretending indifference while secretly shaking every parcel marked with his name.

Five years! He had written during the first year, occasionally during the second, twice during the third. His mother’s letters had followed him patiently from St. Louis to Omaha, from Omaha to Denver, from Denver back to Chicago. He had answered the last with a request for money. She sent it. He had not replied.

Pride is sometimes the mask of dignity and sometimes merely the last possession of a fool. William would not go home until he could go triumphantly. Each failure increased the grandeur required of his return. He would arrive with a book, a fortune, a reputation, a wife, a vindicated life. As these became less probable, return became impossible.

Besides, his family no longer lived in the old house. He had heard that they had moved north, but did not know the address. It was better so. A definite door might have weakened him.

At the river he stopped. Black water showed between plates of ice, and lamps stretched wavering ladders into the darkness. Lake Michigan, he reflected, was broad, cold, and free. One climbed a railing, surrendered a moment to gravity, and all the ineffectual striving was concluded. No more rent, no more hunger, no more interviews with city editors who said, “Leave it; we’ll let you know,” no more waking to discover that consciousness had renewed its lease.

Yet even suicide demands energy.

William looked down and imagined the plunge, the impact, the strangling cold, the animal struggle which would disgrace his philosophical conclusion. He had always disliked cold water. It was characteristic that this trivial aversion should stand between him and eternity.

“Tomorrow, perhaps,” he said.

Then his stomach contracted so violently that he bent against the railing.

A man’s got to eat.

The sentence returned with brutal authority. Death might be arranged later; meanwhile the body mutinied. And if honest methods had failed—if employers would not employ him, friends would not lend to him, pawnbrokers would not accept him—there remained the ancient redistribution of property by personal enterprise.

He would steal.

The decision, once made, warmed him. Not morally; he was too well educated to obtain moral warmth from a sophistry which he saw through while employing it. But action itself has heat. Despair is cold because it is motionless.

He began at once to furnish the crime with arguments. Society had abandoned him. Wealth displayed its insolence in every window. Somewhere, at that very hour, a gentleman was eating too much terrapin and complaining of indigestion, while William Arden, who could explain the historical development of the sonnet, had not a crust. Property was a convention. Hunger was a fact. Jean Valjean had taken bread and achieved respectability in several languages.

The arguments were flimsy, and he knew them to be flimsy. But a man who sincerely desires temptation is seldom delayed by logic.

On State Street the crowd thickened. William studied handbags, coat pockets, unattended parcels. He selected a stout gentleman whose gold watch-chain made an emphatic curve across his waistcoat and followed him half a block. At the decisive instant the gentleman turned into a brilliantly lighted shop, and William, seeing his own white face reflected in the glass, abandoned the enterprise.

“The failure as a pickpocket,” he murmured. “A brief but representative episode.”

Near Washington Street a young woman emerged from a confectioner’s carrying three packages. She was wrapped in dark fur and walked rapidly, looking anxiously for a carriage. One of the packages—a small square box tied with red cord—slipped from beneath her arm and fell unnoticed into the slush.

William saw it. No one else appeared to see.

Here was Providence at last, neatly wrapped and delivered. Jewelry, perhaps; or lace, gloves, silver, something salable before the shops closed. He put his foot over the box.

The young woman continued toward the corner.

William stooped, lifted the package, and examined it. There was no name upon it. His fingers tightened.

Then, with an oath directed against himself, he ran after her.

“I beg your pardon,” he said, touching his hat. “You dropped this.”

She turned with a startled look, saw the box, and uttered a little cry.

“O, thank you! It is my sister’s present. I should not have known where I lost it.”

She smiled and was gone.

William stood staring after her.

“That,” he informed the surrounding metropolis, “was magnificent. I shall starve with an approving conscience.”

But beneath the bitterness something small and stubborn remained alive. He had not taken the parcel. It was an inconvenient discovery. A man preparing to become a criminal prefers not to encounter evidence against his fitness.

He left the crowded business streets and wandered north, where the houses grew larger and the intervals between saloons longer. The rain ceased. A raw wind moved off the lake, scraping clouds from a pale moon. Behind curtained windows families gathered; pianos sounded; shadows crossed ceilings; Christmas trees burned in little private heavens inaccessible to the pavement.

His hatred of wealth grew with his weakness. These houses seemed not merely comfortable but guilty. Their doors were conspiracies, their walls insults. Warmth was hoarded there, and food, and laughter, and the careless security of those who expected tomorrow to resemble today. What right had any man to possess twenty rooms while another walked the street because he lacked the price of one bed?

It did not occur to him that he himself had once possessed such security and thrown it aside. Hunger is a powerful advocate and seldom calls adverse witnesses.

On a quiet street east of Dearborn Avenue he observed a house brilliantly illuminated. Carriages arrived in succession. A servant under a striped awning opened doors; women in pale wraps passed laughing into the vestibule; music flowed from within whenever the great door swung back.

A party.

William paused beneath a bare elm. Houses are most easily entered, he reasoned, when crowded with persons who assume that everyone else has a right to be there. He crossed the street, went down the side passage, and found a service entrance opening as two waiters carried out a crate of bottles.

Neither looked at him.

He entered.

The warmth struck him almost senseless. For several seconds he stood in a corridor filled with the odor of coffee, flowers, roasted meats, damp furs, and evergreen. Servants hurried past. From beyond a baize door came the clatter of dishes and the commanding voice of a cook. A maid glanced at him, but his bearing, so obstinately superior to his clothes, confused her.

“Gentlemen’s dressing-room upstairs?” he asked.

“Second floor, front,” she answered, and fled with a tray.

He removed his hat.

The action was instinctive. He had entered to rob the house, yet somewhere beneath hunger, bitterness, and rags, the boy trained by a careful mother still knew that a gentleman did not wear his hat indoors.

He ascended the back stairs, his heart beating now with great, almost joyous violence. This was action! This was the Dance of Death, with an orchestra below and supper afterward if the dancers were obliging. Childe Roland to the dark tower came, though Childe Roland’s boots were probably dry.

On the second floor he found a long hall. The front rooms had been opened for wraps, and voices sounded nearby. He moved in the opposite direction, trying doors until one yielded.

It was a bedroom, large, quiet, and dimly lighted by a shaded lamp. A fire burned low upon the hearth. The noise of the party reached it as a softened murmur.

William closed the door and stood listening.

No alarm.

He began his search rapidly. A jewel case lay upon the dressing-table, but contained only hairpins. A drawer yielded handkerchiefs, ribbons, letters. Another was locked. He tried the wardrobe, found gowns, and searched their pockets with trembling hands. Shame had become physical, a heat in his face; yet hunger drove him on.

At last, beneath a folded lace collar, he found a small leather box. Inside lay a brooch set with pearls, two rings, and a gold bracelet.

He stared at them.

The moment had come. He was a thief now—not in intention, not in rhetoric, but in fact. The distinction is enormous. Many persons entertain sin as they entertain a notorious visitor, amused by his conversation and confident of their power to dismiss him. They are surprised when he removes his coat and settles by the fire.

William thrust the box into his pocket.

A sound in the hall froze him. Someone passed. He waited, scarcely breathing.

When silence returned he opened another drawer, thinking that, having crossed the line, he might as well cross it profitably. Silver glimmered beneath embroidered linen: a brush, a hand mirror, several small articles. Among them stood a cup, tarnished about the handle but polished across its face.

He took it up.

On the side, in worn Gothic letters, was engraved:

WILLIAM ARDEN  
DECEMBER 24, 1872

The room tilted.

He carried the cup to the lamp. There was no mistake. A shallow dent marked the rim where he had dropped it upon the nursery hearth at seven years old. He remembered his mother scolding the careless nurse and secretly assuring him that the dent improved it. He remembered drinking warm milk from it on birthdays; remembered floating a walnut-shell boat in it; remembered packing it among his treasures before he went to school.

His cup.

He looked about the room with new eyes. The carved dressing-table had belonged to his grandmother. The watercolor above the fire—a foolish blue Italian lake—had hung in the old guest-room. Upon a chair lay his mother’s gray shawl.

He had entered his father’s house.

Coincidence, that sober persons call impossible and life employs whenever it pleases, had led him through a city of more than a million souls, through cold, hunger, pride, and crime, to this room.

The cup fell from his hand upon the carpet.

The door opened.

A woman entered and stopped.

She was nearly fifty, though the light in her face denied arithmetic. Her hair, once dark, had silvered at the temples; her gown was black velvet, and at her throat she wore the old cameo William remembered touching as a child. She looked first at the cup, then at the shabby stranger beside her dressing-table.

“William,” she said.

He had imagined this meeting many times. In one version he was famous and forgave them nobly; in another he was dying and spoke with poetic restraint; in a third he passed his father in the street and gave no sign. Never had he imagined himself standing in his mother’s bedroom with her jewels in his pocket.

“Mother.”

She crossed the room and put both arms around him.

He did not return the embrace. His hands hung at his sides; his body became rigid with terror and shame. But she held him with a strength which seemed to deny the five vanished years.

“My boy,” she said. “My boy—my boy!”

“Don’t.” His voice broke. “For God’s sake, don’t do that.”

She drew back only far enough to see his face. Her eyes moved over the hollow cheeks, the wet coat, the frayed collar.

“You are cold.”

“Mother, listen to me.”

“And starving.”

“I came here to rob the house.”

“Yes, dear.”

The simple answer confounded him.

“I did not know it was yours. I came in from the street. I searched your drawers. I have your jewelry in my pocket.”

He took out the leather box and placed it upon the table. His hand shook so violently that the bracelet slipped to the floor.

“Now you understand.”

She looked at the box and then at him.

“How could you rob your own house?”

He laughed—a harsh, brief sound. “That is sentiment, not law.”

“It is truth.”

“I am a thief.”

“You are my son.”

“I have lied to you. I took money from you. I disappeared. I have done nothing—nothing worth doing. I have failed at everything I touched, and tonight I decided to add burglary to the list.”

She lifted her hands to his face.

“You came home.”

“By accident!”

“Perhaps,” she said. “There are accidents that know more than we do.”

Then he began to struggle, not against her hands, but against the tenderness in them. Accusation he could have met; reproach would have restored his self-command; pardon might have permitted some dignified abasement. But this immediate, unreasoning possession of him—this refusal to recognize the barriers he had labored five years to build—broke his defenses.

“You don’t know what I have been.”

“I know what you are.”

“You know nothing!”

“I know you are hungry.”

At that he bowed his head.

The party continued below. A waltz began, light and measured, while in the quiet room the ruined young man stood beneath his mother’s hands and wept with the shameful abandonment of a child.

She waited. Mothers learn early that certain griefs must expend themselves like storms; to question the thunder is useless.

When he had grown quiet, she said, “Sit by the fire.”

“I cannot stay.”

“You cannot go.”

“Father—”

“Yes,” she said.

The one word sobered him. He turned toward the door.

She caught his sleeve. “William.”

“He will call the police, and perhaps he should.”

“Your father will do no such thing.”

“You do not know him.”

A faint smile touched her mouth. “I have known him for thirty years.”

“He told me never to return until I could return honestly.”

“He has repented those words every day.”

“He does not repent.”

“He does not speak. Men often confuse the two.”

She led him to a chair and rang the bell. When a maid appeared, the mother stood so that William was partly hidden.

“Bring a tray here at once—soup, meat, bread, coffee, whatever is ready. And tell Mr. Arden I wish to see him.”

William rose.

“Sit down,” she commanded.

The old authority remained in her voice. He sat.

His father entered five minutes later.

James Arden was a tall, heavy man with iron-gray whiskers and a forehead that seemed constructed for opposition. He had grown older more honestly than his wife; time showed in every line. He closed the door, looked at William, and became perfectly still.

No one spoke.

The silence between father and son contained five years of anger: the abandoned position, the debts paid secretly, the insolent letters, the unanswered appeals, the pride of one man and the dissipation of the other. Love was there also, but love in some masculine natures lies buried beneath so much fear of expression that it resembles hostility.

Mrs. Arden went to her husband.

“I have found our boy.”

His eyes did not leave William. “So I see.”

“He is ill and hungry.”

William stood. “I entered the house without knowing it was yours. I stole jewelry from that room. I have returned it. If you wish me to leave, I shall leave.”

Mr. Arden’s face hardened, perhaps because it was in danger of doing something else.

“You chose an extraordinary manner of visiting us.”

“I have developed a taste for dramatic entrances.”

The old flippancy escaped before William could prevent it. His father’s brows contracted. Then, unexpectedly, the elder man sighed.

“Still making jokes when you are afraid?”

William stared at him.

His mother placed her hand upon her husband’s arm. “James, tonight is Christmas Eve.”

“I am aware of the date.”

“It is his birthday.”

“I am aware of that also.”

“He has come home.”

“He says he came to steal.”

“Then he chose his own property. We can hardly prosecute him for bad judgment.”

“This is not a matter for wit, Margaret.”

“No. It is a matter for love.”

Mr. Arden walked to the fire and stood with his back to them. Below, the waltz ended in applause.

At last he said, “Leave us alone.”

Mrs. Arden hesitated.

“Please.”

She went to William, kissed his forehead, and whispered, “Do not be proud now, my son. Pride has had five years.”

Then she left them.

The father and son remained standing.

“You look badly,” Mr. Arden said.

“I am not at my best.”

“Sit down.”

William obeyed.

His father paced once across the room. “Your mother believes I drove you away.”

“I drove myself.”

“I told you to go.”

“I gave you reason.”

“I expected you to come back within a week.”

“I expected to come back within a year, with a fortune.”

“A very foolish expectation.”

“Yes.”

Another silence followed. Men who can negotiate contracts, command employees, address committees, and dictate opinions upon every public subject may find three honest words to a son beyond their eloquence.

Mr. Arden took up the silver cup.

“You used to drink from this.”

“I remember.”

“You threw it at the cat once.”

“I missed.”

“You broke a window.”

“Yes.”

“Your mother said the cat had jumped against the glass.”

William looked toward him. “I never knew that.”

“She lied badly. Your mother has many virtues, but no talent for deception.”

The father set down the cup.

“I followed your career as well as I could.”

“There was not much to follow.”

“I read your articles.”

“Three of them?”

“More than three.”

“Then you read some under names I no longer remember.”

“One about the stockyards was good.”

“The editor paid me seven dollars.”

“It was worth ten.”

William almost smiled.

His father turned suddenly. The sternness was still present, but behind it stood fatigue—deep, accumulated fatigue.

“I was hard with you,” he said. “You were idle, vain, unreliable, and insolent.”

“All true.”

“But I was hard. I thought strength could be beaten into a man as a nail is beaten into oak. When you bent, I struck harder. When you broke away, I called it proof of weakness.”

“You were not responsible for what followed.”

“I was responsible for being your father.”

William lowered his eyes.

“I failed with you,” the older man said.

The word passed between them with strange power. William had considered failure his private brand, burned upon him alone. To hear it from this successful, respected, inflexible man altered its meaning. Perhaps failure was not a final species of being; perhaps it was an act, a season, an error shared even by the strong.

“I failed more thoroughly,” William said.

“We need not compete in it.”

His father approached and held out his hand.

“You may stay.”

William looked at the hand but did not take it.

“On probation?” he asked.

“No.”

“Until I find employment?”

“As long as you need a home.”

“I have debts.”

“We shall discuss them.”

“I may disappoint you again.”

“I dare say you will.”

“And you may regret this tomorrow.”

“I have regretted enough yesterdays.”

William rose slowly. Their hands met. The father’s grip was firm, then tightened painfully.

“Your mother has suffered,” he said.

“I know.”

“No, you do not. But you may learn.”

He released the hand and turned away. At the door he stopped.

“One thing more. Did you take anything else?”

“No.”

“Good. A man may begin again from many places. Prison is an inconvenient one.”

Then he went out.

William remained by the fire, looking at the closed door. It had not been an embrace. It had not been complete understanding, complete absolution, or the sudden conversion of two unlike natures into harmonious affection. Life seldom supplies such completions. Yet a hand had crossed the gulf.

That was enough.

The door opened almost immediately, and Mrs. Arden entered behind a servant bearing a tray. She dismissed the girl, locked the door, and arranged the food herself.

There was soup, clear and steaming; slices of turkey; potatoes browned in butter; celery; bread; cranberry jelly; coffee; and a wedge of mince-pie. The abundance was almost terrible. William looked at it with the solemnity of a worshiper before an altar.

“Slowly,” his mother said.

He tried to obey. The first spoonful of soup caused a pain so sharp that he stopped. She waited, watching him, then gave him another. Gradually the frozen machinery of the body accepted life. Warmth entered his chest, spread through his limbs, softened the rigid muscles of his face.

He ate.

This simple act was the seal of his restoration. Men may make promises, exchange pardons, utter creeds; but he who sits at a family table and is fed has been admitted again into the fellowship of the living.

His mother buttered bread as she had when he was ten.

“Do you remember,” she said, “the birthday when you demanded oysters for breakfast, chocolate at noon, and plum-pudding for supper?”

“I was sick all night.”

“Your father said it would teach you moderation.”

“It did not.”

“No,” she answered gravely, “I observed that.”

He glanced at her and saw the smile in her eyes. For a moment the five years vanished so completely that he expected to hear the nursery clock.

When he had eaten enough to make hunger less a madness than an ache, shame returned.

“Mother, you must let me tell you everything.”

“Not tonight.”

“You do not know what you are taking back.”

“My son.”

“That is a word, not an account.”

“It is the only account I require.”

“I have been cowardly. I have lived on friends poorer than myself. I have written things I did not believe, praised men I despised, and borrowed money I knew I could not repay. Once, in Denver—”

She laid a finger upon his lips.

“No.”

“You cannot forgive without knowing.”

“I do not forgive you.”

He recoiled.

She drew his head against her shoulder.

“Forgiveness is for strangers,” she said. “For persons who stand outside and have wronged us. You are not outside. You are mine. Do you ask your hand to pardon your wounded foot? It suffers with it. I have suffered with you, though you would not let me come near.”

“But I wronged you.”

“Yes.”

“And you ask no explanation?”

“Love does not always need explanations. It waits beneath them. It waits while anger talks, while pride travels, while folly spends itself. It waits and waits and waits.”

“Even when there is nothing worth loving?”

“My boy, love does not make inventories.”

He could not answer. He knelt beside her, hiding his face in her lap, and she bent over him, stroking his wet hair.

After a time she made him remove his coat. She found dry clothing that had belonged to a cousin staying in the house, sent for stockings and slippers, and would have summoned a physician had he not protested with genuine alarm. When he was warm and clean, she led him downstairs by a private stair to the library, away from the guests.

The room had been furnished with objects from the old home. His father’s books stood behind glass; the brass clock ticked upon the mantel; a faded rug retained the scorch made by a Christmas spark when William was twelve. And beside the hearth was the low leather chair in which he had read Scott, dreamed of heroic careers, and fallen asleep over Latin grammar.

He touched its worn arm.

“We kept it for you,” his mother said.

“You kept everything.”

“Not everything.”

The words held no reproach. That made them harder to bear.

He sat in the chair. It had become smaller, or he larger, but it received him with the familiarity of an old servant. His mother placed a rug over his knees.

From the drawing-room came laughter, music, the pleasant confusion of a prosperous Christmas party. No one there knew that the lost son had entered through the kitchen and been born again beside a stolen cup. Presently his father appeared at the library door.

“The guests are leaving,” he said to his wife. “They are asking for you.”

“Let them ask.”

“You should go down for a few minutes.”

She looked at William.

“I shall not vanish,” he said.

She kissed him and went.

Mr. Arden remained. He adjusted a log with the poker, though the fire required no adjustment.

“I have told the servants you arrived unexpectedly from the West,” he said.

“That is true in spirit, if not direction.”

“Tomorrow we will decide what is to be said.”

“Tomorrow,” William repeated.

It was a word he had nearly surrendered at the river.

His father glanced toward him. “There will be time.”

“Yes.”

He went out, closing the door softly.

William leaned back. The food had produced a delicious heaviness, the fire a luxury almost painful. Safety, when it returns after long absence, is not immediately believed. He listened for the knock of a policeman, the command to leave, the awakening in some frozen hallway. None came.

The clock ticked. The logs settled. Outside, carriage wheels diminished one by one.

Near midnight the bells began.

They sounded from steeples across the city, some deep and solemn, some thin in the windy distance, all confused by space into one immense trembling music. They rang above the lake and the river, above saloons and churches, above hotels where strangers feasted, hospitals where strangers died, stations where men departed, tenements where children slept hungry, and warm houses where forgotten chairs waited through the years.

William opened his eyes. His mother sat beside him, her hand resting upon his.

“Is it midnight?” he asked.

“Yes. Christmas Day.”

“My birthday is over.”

“No,” she said. “I think it has just begun.”

He smiled faintly and closed his eyes again.

Perhaps the life of man is not a straight account in which every waste must remain waste and every error be carried forward until the final sum. Perhaps there are powers—human, divine, or so intermingled that only pride insists upon distinguishing them—which gather broken things and refuse to call them useless. The clay may be marred beneath its own foolish pressure; yet the Potter does not therefore cast it from the wheel. He wets it with tears, presses it again, and from the distortion shapes some humbler vessel.

These are hopes, not certainties. But hope was enough for William Arden that night.

He slept beside the fire, his face thin and tired, his future unwritten. His mother watched him as she had watched him in infancy, before ambition, failure, hunger, and shame had acquired their names. Beyond the curtained windows the snow began again, covering wheel-tracks, soot, and the black scars of the street with a whiteness that would not last, but was beautiful before morning.

And when dawn came pale over Chicago, it found him still at home.

# The Lighthouse Keeper’s Last Guest

On the morning the sea returned the red boat, Elias Vale was repairing the lighthouse clock.

The clock had not told the correct time in twenty-three years. Its face hung above the spiral staircase, visible from every floor, and its hands had stopped at seventeen minutes past four on the night Elias’s daughter disappeared.

Most people would have replaced it. Elias could not.

He sat on the stairs with a screwdriver between his teeth and the brass casing balanced on his knees. Outside, rain pressed against the windows. Wind prowled around the tower, moaning through cracks in the stone.

Then came three knocks at the lighthouse door.

Elias looked toward the entrance.

No one visited Blackglass Island in November. The supply boat had come four days earlier, and the fishermen from the mainland knew better than to cross the channel in a storm.

The knocks came again.

Three, slow and deliberate.

Elias tucked the screwdriver into his pocket and descended. When he opened the door, cold rain rushed over his boots.

A young woman stood on the step.

She wore a yellow coat, soaked dark at the shoulders, and held one hand against the doorframe to steady herself. Her black hair clung to her cheeks. She was perhaps twenty-five, though exhaustion had added shadows beneath her eyes.

Behind her, drawn halfway onto the rocks, was a little red boat.

Elias stared at it.

“Please,” the woman said. “May I come in?”

He stepped aside.

She entered, bringing with her the smell of rain, salt, and something faintly metallic. Elias closed the door and slid the iron bolt into place.

“There’s a fire upstairs,” he said. “You’ll want to get warm.”

The woman removed her coat. Beneath it she wore a gray sweater and a silver pendant shaped like a crescent moon.

Elias stopped breathing for a moment.

His daughter had owned a pendant exactly like it.

The woman noticed his expression and covered the necklace with her hand.

“Is something wrong?”

“No.”

“You looked as if you’d seen a ghost.”

“People often mistake memory for one.”

She studied him, uncertain whether he had made a joke. Then she followed him up the winding stairs.

The lighthouse kitchen occupied the second floor. It was a circular room with a coal stove, a narrow table, and shelves crowded with jars. Elias gave the woman a blanket and set water to boil.

“What’s your name?” he asked.

“Mara.”

He nearly dropped the kettle.

The woman frowned. “Are you all right?”

Elias placed the kettle firmly on the stove.

“My daughter was called Mara.”

“Oh.” She drew the blanket tighter. “I’m sorry.”

“Why?”

“You said ‘was.’”

The storm struck the tower with a sudden gust. Cups rattled in their hooks.

Elias looked out the window. Waves shattered white against the black cliffs.

“How did you get here?”

“In the boat.”

“I can see that.”

“I don’t remember much else.”

“Where did you launch from?”

“I don’t know.”

“You crossed the Blackglass Channel in that thing during a storm, but you don’t know where you came from?”

Mara looked down at her hands.

“I woke up in the boat,” she said. “There was water around my ankles. I saw the lighthouse and rowed toward it.”

“You rowed?”

“Yes.”

“There are no oars.”

Silence entered the room.

Elias took the lamp from the table and descended to the entrance. Through the thick glass of the door, he could see the red boat grinding against the rocks.

No oars lay inside it.

No rope, sail, or engine. Nothing that could have brought it across the channel.

When he returned, Mara was standing before the old clock.

“Why did it stop?” she asked.

“It broke.”

“At four seventeen.”

“That is what the hands suggest.”

She touched the brass rim.

The clock ticked.

Elias froze.

A second tick followed, then a third.

The minute hand trembled and moved forward.

Mara snatched her fingers away.

The clock stopped.

Neither of them spoke.

At last, Elias went to the cupboard, took out a bottle of brandy, and poured a small measure into his tea.

“Perhaps,” Mara said, “I should explain.”

“That would be welcome.”

“I’ve been having dreams.”

“So have I. Mine usually involve unpaid bills.”

“I’m serious.”

“So am I.”

She returned to the table but did not sit.

“For months, I’ve dreamed about this lighthouse. I’d never seen it before, yet I knew every room. I knew there was a crack in the third step from the top. I knew the lantern glass had a bullet mark on the western side.”

Elias said nothing.

Both things were true.

“In the dreams,” she continued, “someone was calling me from under the water. Last night the voice became clear.”

“What did it say?”

“Come home.”

The wind moaned against the walls.

Elias drank the brandy without tasting it.

“This island is not your home.”

“I know.”

“Where do you live?”

“Bellweather.”

“That’s two hundred miles north.”

“I have a flat above a bakery. I restore old paintings at the city museum. My mother’s name is Jean, my father’s name is Thomas, and I have a cat called Bishop who hates everyone except the postman.” Her words came quickly, as if she were reciting evidence. “I know who I am.”

“Then why are you here?”

“I hoped you could tell me.”

Elias looked toward the clock.

Its hands still pointed to seventeen minutes past four.

Twenty-three years earlier, his daughter had left the lighthouse in a red boat.

She had been nineteen, furious, and determined to reach the mainland despite an approaching storm. They had argued at the door. Elias remembered each word because grief had carved them into him.

You cannot command the sea, Mara had shouted.

No, he had replied, but while you live under my roof, I can command you.

Then I won’t live under your roof.

She had taken the boat. Elias had watched its red hull vanish between walls of rain.

At four seventeen in the afternoon, lightning struck the tower. The clock stopped. The lantern failed for nine minutes.

The coast guard found pieces of the boat the following day.

They never found Mara.

Now a young woman with her name and necklace had arrived in another red boat that could not possibly have crossed the channel.

Elias poured a second brandy.

“I think you should leave when the storm clears,” he said.

Mara stared at him. “That’s all?”

“That’s enough.”

“You know something.”

“I know storms make fools of sailors.”

“I’m not a sailor.”

“Clearly.”

She flinched at his sharpness. Elias regretted it but offered no apology.

The storm continued through the afternoon. By evening, the channel had disappeared beneath rain and darkness. Elias lit the great lantern at the top of the tower. Its beam swept across the sea, vanished, and returned.

Mara wandered through the lighthouse.

She knew where things were.

She found spare candles in a drawer she had never opened. She avoided the loose board beside the bedroom door. When Elias asked her to fetch a wrench, she went directly to a cabinet on the fourth floor.

Each small certainty made him colder.

After supper, Mara sat beside the stove while Elias washed their bowls.

“What was she like?” she asked.

“Who?”

“Your daughter.”

He scrubbed a bowl that was already clean.

“Stubborn.”

“That sounds like something a stubborn father would say.”

“She was reckless. Impatient. Always asking questions and never listening to the answers.”

Mara smiled faintly. “Anything good?”

“She could whistle any song after hearing it once. She rescued moths from candle flames. She believed there was no machine that couldn’t be repaired if you understood why it had broken.”

“That last part sounds like you.”

“No. I believe some things stay broken.”

The lighthouse clock gave a single tick.

Elias turned.

Its hands had not moved.

Mara touched her pendant. “Did that belong to her?”

“Yes.”

“My mother gave it to me when I was a baby. She said it was found wrapped in my blanket.”

“Found where?”

Mara hesitated.

“On a beach near Bellweather.”

The bowl slipped from Elias’s hands and struck the basin. It cracked neatly in two.

“My parents adopted me,” she said. “No one knows where I came from. I was discovered alone just before dawn. The doctors thought I was only a few days old.”

“What date?”

“The twelfth of November.”

Elias gripped the edge of the basin.

Twenty-three years ago, Mara’s boat had vanished on the eleventh of November.

Behind him, the clock began ticking.

This time it did not stop.

The sound filled the kitchen, gentle and ordinary, yet Elias felt it in his bones. The minute hand moved from seventeen past four to eighteen.

At that instant, the lighthouse lantern went dark.

Elias ran.

He took the stairs two at a time, climbing toward the lantern room. Mara followed. Above them, the mechanism groaned as the great lens slowed.

When Elias reached the top, he smelled burned oil. The main wick had gone out, though the fuel reservoir was full. He struck a match. The flame bent sideways in a wind that should not have existed inside the sealed chamber.

Beyond the glass, the sea was black.

Then, far below, something answered with a light of its own.

A pale green glow rose beneath the waves.

It formed a path leading from the island toward the open ocean.

Mara pressed her palms to the glass. “I’ve seen that in my dreams.”

A figure stood at the end of the path.

It was impossibly distant and perfectly clear: a young woman in a white sweater, balanced on the surface of the sea. Her dark hair streamed in the storm. Around her neck gleamed a crescent moon.

Elias struck another match. It went out.

The figure lifted one arm.

Not waving.

Beckoning.

“Mara,” Elias whispered.

Beside him, his guest answered, “Yes?”

But he had not been speaking to her.

The figure on the water turned and walked toward the horizon. The green path began to fade behind her.

The young woman in the lantern room grabbed the door handle.

Elias caught her wrist.

“Let me go.”

“No.”

“She wants me to follow.”

“And you intend to?”

“I need to know.”

“I know what waits in the sea.”

“You don’t know anything.”

“I know it took my daughter.”

Mara pulled against his grip. “What if it didn’t?”

The clock chimed below them.

Once.

Twice.

It had no bell, yet the sound rolled through the tower.

With every chime, Elias saw a fragment of another night.

Mara as a child, sleeping beneath his coat while he polished the lantern glass.

Mara at twelve, standing on the rocks with both arms spread, pretending to command the gulls.

Mara at nineteen, her face bright with anger.

Then I won’t live under your roof.

Three.

Four.

The tower shuddered.

A crack appeared in the lantern glass, racing from the old bullet mark to the ceiling.

Five.

Mara twisted free and ran down the stairs.

Elias followed, shouting her name. She reached the entrance before him, pulled back the bolt, and opened the door.

Wind exploded into the lighthouse.

The red boat waited on the rocks.

The green path had reached the shore.

Mara stepped into the rain.

Elias caught her at the water’s edge.

“Listen to me!” he shouted.

The sea surged around their ankles, though they stood well above the ordinary tide.

The distant figure had stopped walking. She watched them from the horizon.

Mara turned on Elias. Rain streamed down her face.

“She’s calling me.”

“She called me too.”

“What?”

“Every night for twenty-three years.” He struggled to make himself heard above the waves. “I dreamed of her beneath the water. Sometimes she begged me to follow. Sometimes she promised I could change what happened. But grief promises many things.”

“This is different.”

“No. It only feels different because it has learned your name.”

Mara looked toward the glowing road.

“I have to know who I am.”

“You told me already. You restore paintings. You live above a bakery. You have a hateful cat.”

“That isn’t enough.”

“It is everything.”

The figure on the sea raised both arms.

The water beside the island rose into the shape of a wall. Within it, faces appeared—pale, wavering faces of sailors and passengers, children and old men, all those the Blackglass Channel had taken.

Among them was Elias’s daughter.

Not as she had been at nineteen, but older.

She looked almost exactly like the woman standing beside him.

Elias’s heart broke with such force that he staggered.

The face in the wave opened its eyes.

“Father,” it said.

The voice was not loud. It did not need to be.

Elias stepped forward.

Mara seized his hand. “Don’t.”

His daughter smiled from within the water.

“I waited,” she said.

Elias felt the years fall away. He was no longer an old man on a freezing shore. He was a father standing in a doorway, one apology away from preventing the worst mistake of his life.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

The face came closer.

“You can tell me.”

“I should have stopped you.”

“You tried.”

“I should have gone after you.”

“Yes.”

The word entered him like a blade.

The wall of water leaned over the rocks.

Mara pulled at his arm. “That isn’t her.”

But Elias wanted it to be. Want was a tide stronger than reason. He saw his daughter’s hand extend from the wave, white and open.

“Come home,” she said.

Home.

He took another step.

The water closed over his boots.

Then the young woman beside him began to whistle.

The tune was thin and shaking at first, nearly lost in the storm. Elias recognized it after three notes.

It was an old harbor song. He had sung it when his daughter was small, and she had whistled it whenever she was afraid.

Elias turned.

Mara’s eyes were shut. Tears mixed with rain on her cheeks, but she kept whistling.

The face in the wave changed.

For an instant, it became furious. Its mouth stretched too wide, and darkness poured from its eyes.

Elias understood.

Memory could wound him, but it had never been cruel. Whatever wore his daughter’s face had chosen the one word she would not have said.

Yes.

His Mara would not have blamed him, even if he deserved it.

Especially then.

Elias stepped backward.

“You are not my daughter.”

The sea roared.

The wall collapsed.

Water swept across the rocks, knocking Elias down. Mara caught his coat, but the current dragged them both toward the edge. The red boat spun past, struck the cliff, and shattered.

Elias clawed at the stone. His fingers slipped.

Mara’s pendant snagged in a crack.

The silver chain snapped tight around her throat.

For one terrible second, it held them.

Elias reached up and closed his hand around the crescent. The metal felt warm. Images flooded his mind—not dreams, not memories, but something stranger.

His daughter in the red boat.

Lightning striking the sea.

A wave opening like a door.

Mara sinking into green light, the silver pendant floating above her.

Then a newborn child crying on a distant beach at dawn.

Time folding.

A life ending and beginning at once.

Elias tore the pendant free from the rock. The chain broke, but he managed to seize Mara’s wrist. Together they crawled beyond the reach of the waves.

Behind them, the green path vanished.

The figure at the horizon remained for a moment longer.

It was no longer a drowned woman or a hungry thing. It was only a shadow.

Then the lighthouse beam returned, sweeping across the water, and the shadow was gone.

Dawn found Elias and Mara sitting on the kitchen floor, wrapped in blankets.

The clock showed six forty-two.

It ticked steadily.

Neither had spoken for a long time.

At last Mara placed the broken pendant on the table.

“Was I her?” she asked.

Elias watched steam rise from his tea.

“I don’t know.”

“You saw something when you touched it.”

“So did you.”

She nodded. “I remember the storm. But I also remember my mother teaching me to read. I remember breaking my arm when I was seven. I remember my first day at the museum.”

“Then those memories are yours.”

“And the others?”

“Also yours, perhaps.”

“That makes no sense.”

“The sea rarely does.”

Mara picked up the crescent. “If I am your daughter—”

“You are not.”

She looked wounded.

Elias continued more gently. “And you are. Maybe some part of her crossed the water. Maybe time gave her another shore. But the woman my daughter might have become is not a debt you owe me.”

Mara stared at the old man across the table.

“What if I want you to be my father?”

Elias looked down.

For twenty-three years, he had imagined this moment in a thousand forms. In every version he begged forgiveness, and his daughter granted it. The fantasy had always ended there. He had never considered what came after forgiveness, because grief was easier to preserve than a life.

“I was not very good at it,” he said.

“So you’ve had time to practice.”

He laughed then, unexpectedly and painfully. Mara laughed too.

Outside, the storm moved east. Sunlight broke through the clouds and touched the wet stones, making the island shine.

The mainland rescue boat arrived before noon. Its captain found the remains of the red boat scattered along the rocks and demanded to know how Mara had crossed the channel.

She looked at Elias.

“I got lost,” she said.

The captain stared at the wreckage. “In a boat with no oars?”

“Very lost.”

Before she boarded, Mara wrote her address on the back of an old supply receipt.

“You could visit,” she said. “Bellweather has an excellent museum.”

“I dislike cities.”

“There’s a maritime gallery.”

“I dislike galleries.”

“And a bakery.”

Elias took the paper. “I will consider the bakery.”

Mara smiled. Around her neck hung the crescent pendant on a piece of lighthouse cord.

As the rescue boat pulled away, she stood at the stern and whistled the harbor song. Elias listened until the distance swallowed it.

Winter passed.

The lighthouse clock continued to keep time. Elias no longer repaired it, though every morning he paused beneath its face to hear the ticking.

In March, he packed a small suitcase.

He left detailed instructions for the temporary keeper, locked the tower door, and boarded the supply boat for the mainland. From there he took two trains north.

Bellweather was larger than he expected and louder than seemed necessary. He became lost twice before finding the bakery. Above it was a blue door with a brass knocker.

Elias climbed the stairs.

Before he could knock, the door opened.

Mara stood there, smiling. A large gray cat glared at him from behind her legs.

“You came,” she said.

“I said I would consider the bakery.”

“Of course.”

She stepped aside.

On the wall behind her hung a newly restored painting of Blackglass Lighthouse beneath a clear morning sky. A red boat rested safely on the shore.

Elias entered.

The cat hissed.

From somewhere in the apartment, a clock chimed four seventeen, then continued on to four eighteen.

This time, Elias did not look back.
